P=[∗23−23∗2313∗1323] Consider the matrix P shown above. Given that A=PDPT is an orthogonal diagonalization of a 3×3 symmetric matrix A for some diagonal matrix D, which of the following could be the first column of the matrix P?

a
[0−2222]
b
[1323−23]
c
[0−11]
d
[1−22]
e
[13−2323]
Submit

decision.explanation: In an orthogonal diagonalization, the columns of P must be orthonormal. Option e has squared norm (1+4+4)/9=1 and dot products (2−4+2)/9=0 and (−2−2+4)/9=0 with the second and third columns, respectively.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}\,∗\, & \frac{2}{3} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ \,∗\, & \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ \,∗\, & \frac{1}{3} & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A$ for some diagonal matrix $D,$ which of the following could be the first column of the matrix $P?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since  $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A,$ the matrix $P$ must be a $3\times 3$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the first column must be orthogonal to the second and third columns, and

- the norm of the first column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

after.html:
Question 1
?

P=[∗23−23∗2313∗1323] Consider the matrix P shown above. Given that A=PDPT is an orthogonal diagonalization of a 3×3 symmetric matrix A for some diagonal matrix D, which of the following could be the first column of the matrix P?

a
[0−2222]
b
[1323−23]
c
[0−11]
d
[1−22]
e
[13−2323]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since A=PDPT is an orthogonal diagonalization of a 3×3 symmetric matrix A, the matrix P must be a 3×3 orthogonal matrix. This means that

  • the first column must be orthogonal to the second and third columns, and

  • the norm of the first column must be equal to 1.

Among the given options, only the vector [13−2323] has both properties.

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Parts of an Orthogonal Diagonalization
content.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}\,∗\, & \frac{2}{3} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ \,∗\, & \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ \,∗\, & \frac{1}{3} & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A$ for some diagonal matrix $D,$ which of the following could be the first column of the matrix $P?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since  $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A,$ the matrix $P$ must be a $3\times 3$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the first column must be orthogonal to the second and third columns, and

- the norm of the first column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

A=[123222321],D=[0000−20006] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that D=PTAP, where P is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix P?

a
[111]
b
[33−3333]
c
[−101]
d
[333333]
e
[22−220]
Submit

decision.explanation: Since AP=PD, the third column must be a unit eigenvector of A with eigenvalue 6. Each row of A sums to 6, so (1,1,1)^T is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 6. Normalizing it gives option d.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix $P?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ Computing $A-6I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{3}.$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm, we obtain the third column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 2
?

A=[123222321],D=[0000−20006] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that D=PTAP, where P is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix P?

a
[111]
b
[33−3333]
c
[−101]
d
[333333]
e
[22−220]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

D=PTAP.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that A is symmetric and D is diagonal. Therefore, D=PTAP gives an orthogonal diagonalization of A.

From the diagonal matrix D we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are λ1=0, λ2=−2, and λ3=6. So, the third column of P corresponds to the eigenvalue λ3=6.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ3=6. Computing A−6I, we get

A−6I=[123222321]−6[100010001]=[−5232−4232−5].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−6I)x=0 gives the eigenvector

v3=[111],

where ‖v3‖=3. Dividing v3 by its norm, we obtain the third column of P: v3‖v3‖=13[111]=[333333]

verification.explanation: The revealed solution explicitly gives option d: (1,1,1)^T normalized by √3. This agrees with the calculation: the vector has unit norm and satisfies Av=6v, as required for the third column. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option b.

content.knowledge_point: Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix With Distinct Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix $P?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ Computing $A-6I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{3}.$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm, we obtain the third column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{3}.$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm, we obtain the third column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$
history.html:
Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

D=PTAP.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that A is symmetric and D is diagonal. Therefore, D=PTAP gives an orthogonal diagonalization of A.

From the diagonal matrix D we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are λ1=0, λ2=−2, and λ3=6. So, the third column of P corresponds to the eigenvalue λ3=6.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ3=6. Computing A−6I, we get

A−6I=[123222321]−6[100010001]=[−5232−4232−5].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−6I)x=0 gives the eigenvector

v3=[111],

where ‖v3‖=3. Dividing v3 by its norm, we obtain the third column of P: v3‖v3‖=13[111]=[333333]

Your Answer:
[33−3333]

Question 3
?

A=[324202423],D=[−1000−10008] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that D=PTAP, where P is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix P?

a
[10−1] and [020]
b
[−22022] and [010]
c
[−22022] and [−26223−26]
d
[−13023] and [−26223−26]
e
[220−22] and [−3333−63]
Submit

decision.explanation: The first two columns must be orthonormal eigenvectors for eigenvalue −1. Since (A+I)v=0 reduces to 2x+y+2z=0, both vectors in option c satisfy this equation. Each has squared norm 1, and their dot product is 0, so they can be the first two columns of P.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix $P?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=8.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
{e}_{1}={v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

and we find ${e}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\frac{{v}_{2}\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\  & ={v}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{e}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, dividing ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}_{1}}{‖{e}_{1}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{e}_{2}}{‖{e}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{9}{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6} \\ \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

Question 3
?

A=[324202423],D=[−1000−10008] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that D=PTAP, where P is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix P?

a
[10−1] and [020]
b
[−22022] and [010]
c
[−22022] and [−26223−26]
d
[−13023] and [−26223−26]
e
[220−22] and [−3333−63]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

D=PTAP.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that A is symmetric and D is diagonal. Therefore, D=PTAP gives an orthogonal diagonalization of A.

From the diagonal matrix D we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are λ1=−1, λ2=−1, and λ3=8. So, the first and second columns of P correspond to the eigenvalue λ1=−1.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ1=λ2=−1. Computing A−(−1)I, we get

A−(−1)I=[324202423]+[100010001]=[424212424].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−1)I)x=0 gives two eigenvectors:

v1=[−101] and v2=[−120]

Notice that eigenvectors v1 and v2 are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set e1=v1=[−101], and we find e2 as follows:

e2=v2−v2⋅e1e1⋅e1e1=v2−12e1=[−120]−12[−101]=[−122−12]

Finally, dividing e1 and e2 by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of P:

e1‖e1‖=12[−101]=[−22022]e2‖e2‖=192[−122−12]=[−26223−26]

content.knowledge_point: Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix $P?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=8.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
{e}_{1}={v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

and we find ${e}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\frac{{v}_{2}\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\  & ={v}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{e}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, dividing ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}_{1}}{‖{e}_{1}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{e}_{2}}{‖{e}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{9}{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6} \\ \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=8.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
{e}_{1}={v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

and we find ${e}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\frac{{v}_{2}\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\  & ={v}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{e}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, dividing ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}_{1}}{‖{e}_{1}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{e}_{2}}{‖{e}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{9}{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6} \\ \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since AP=PD, the third column must be a unit eigenvector with eigenvalue 4. Solving (A−4I)v=0 gives x=y and z=0. Option e has this form, has norm 1, and satisfies Av=4v.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix $P?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ Computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2}.$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm, we obtain the third column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 4

A=[130310000],D=[−200000004] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that D=PTAP, where P is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix P?

a
[33−3333]
b
[0−2222]
c
[13−2313]
d
[0−1212]
e
[22220]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

D=PTAP.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that A is symmetric and D is diagonal. Therefore, D=PTAP gives an orthogonal diagonalization of A.

From the diagonal matrix D we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are λ1=−2, λ2=0, and λ3=4. So, the third column of P corresponds to the eigenvalue λ3=4.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ3=4. Computing A−4I, we get

A−4I=[130310000]−4[100010001]=[−3303−3000−4].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector

v3=[110],

where ‖v3‖=2. Dividing v3 by its norm, we obtain the third column of P: v3‖v3‖=12[110]=[22220]

verification.explanation: The revealed worked solution declares option e, obtained by normalizing (1,1,0)^T. Independently, this vector has unit norm and satisfies Av=4v, as required for the third column. The incorrect feedback refers to the deliberately submitted option a.

content.knowledge_point: Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix With Distinct Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix $P?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ Computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2}.$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm, we obtain the third column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 5
?

A=[7−12−17−22−210],D=[6000600012] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that D=PTAP, where P is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix P?

a
[2550−255] and [010]
b
[−255055] and [10102221010]
c
[−255055] and [30303063015]
d
[−201] and [110]
e
[20−22] and [663626]
Submit

decision.explanation: The first two columns must be orthonormal eigenvectors with eigenvalue 6. The equation (A−6I)v=0 reduces to x−y+2z=0. Both vectors in option c satisfy this equation, each has norm 1, and their dot product is 0.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 7 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 12\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix $P?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=6,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=12.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2}.$ 

Now, we need to find eigenvectors that correspond to ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=6.$ Computing $A-6I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 7 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
{e}_{1}={v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

and we find ${e}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\frac{{v}_{2}\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\  & ={v}_{2}+\frac{2}{5}{e}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+\frac{2}{5}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ 1 \\ \frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, dividing ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}_{1}}{‖{e}_{1}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{e}_{2}}{‖{e}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{(\frac{\sqrt{30}}{5})}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ 1 \\ \frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{30}}{30} \\ \frac{\sqrt{30}}{6} \\ \frac{\sqrt{30}}{15}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

A=[7−12−17−22−210],D=[6000600012] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that D=PTAP, where P is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix P?

a
[2550−255] and [010]
b
[−255055] and [10102221010]
c
[−255055] and [30303063015]
d
[−201] and [110]
e
[20−22] and [663626]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

D=PTAP.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that A is symmetric and D is diagonal. Therefore, D=PTAP gives an orthogonal diagonalization of A.

From the diagonal matrix D we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are λ1=6, λ2=6, and λ3=12. So, the first and second columns of P correspond to the eigenvalues λ1 and λ2.

Now, we need to find eigenvectors that correspond to λ1=λ2=6. Computing A−6I, we get

A−6I=[7−12−17−22−210]−6[100010001]=[1−12−11−22−24].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−6I)x=0 gives two eigenvectors:

v1=[−201] and v2=[110]

Notice that eigenvectors v1 and v2 are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set e1=v1=[−201], and we find e2 as follows:

e2=v2−v2⋅e1e1⋅e1e1=v2+25e1=[110]+25[−201]=[15125]

Finally, dividing e1 and e2 by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of P:

e1‖e1‖=15[−201]=[−255055]e2‖e2‖=1(305)[15125]=[30303063015]

content.knowledge_point: Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 7 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 12\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix $P?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=6,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=12.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2}.$ 

Now, we need to find eigenvectors that correspond to ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=6.$ Computing $A-6I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 7 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
{e}_{1}={v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

and we find ${e}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\frac{{v}_{2}\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\  & ={v}_{2}+\frac{2}{5}{e}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+\frac{2}{5}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ 1 \\ \frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, dividing ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}_{1}}{‖{e}_{1}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{e}_{2}}{‖{e}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{(\frac{\sqrt{30}}{5})}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ 1 \\ \frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{30}}{30} \\ \frac{\sqrt{30}}{6} \\ \frac{\sqrt{30}}{15}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
